title: Why are so many services using email magic links for login?
summary:
I've noticed a big uptick in login screens defaulting to sending email magic links rather than asking for a password. Notably Claude does this (which during the Outlook outage last week completely blocked me from accessing it).

I can only assume that this is a misguided attempt to make login easier for the people who use the Forgot Password link all the the time instead of a proper password manager.

It's 1FA where your single factor is access a different service (your email) rather than a known secret.

Is there an actual best practice HIG or security guideline that recommends this approach? To my mind, it's both less secure and less convenient. I'm wondering if it's an anti pattern where someone (or an LLM) has copied a service which does this, and that creates a feedback loop where more orgs jump on the bandwagon.

title: Ask HN: How do engineers approach startups that aren't actively hiring?
summary:
I've been trying to find an opportunity in early stage startups.

My approach until now has been to identify startups working on problems that genuinely interest me and where I think I could contribute something to them.

rather than applying through conventional job listings, I've mostly been trying to reach out directly to founders and co-founders through cold emails.

I generally try to make these emails specific to each of them. spend some time understanding what they're building, identify things that could be improved after using their product and sometimes suggest what I can build or contribute to the product.

However, It mostly has been like talking to a wall till now. there has been zero responses to any of the emails I've sent.

this isn't really to vent, but rather to understand what might be going wrong.

well upon looking here and there the general advice I've received is to build good projects or do even more cold emailing. but something feels off I generally build things that are not that conventional its cool in its own nature and carry quite a lot of technical insight while just increasing the amount of cold emails somehow goes against my opinion of (quality >>> quantity)

extra context - I generally avoid roles that are repetitive in work and don't scratch my curious brain for instance that of frontend and backend I just mostly skip them since I have already worked in my last 2 jobs on these. its more of me looking into startups doing niche things.

there are some things I understand already for instance founders already are busy most of the emails saying "Hey I want a job" generally are more or less ignored so I shifted to the approach of making the subject line about something I thought could be improved in their product.

I also understand that most of the founders won't risk it with some new guy who is just saying that he can work on this or can build this. It's understandable from this POV, but then the entire cold emailing logic breaks apart if this is taken into consideration.

P.S. Both backend and frontend can go incredibly deep. I didn't mean that they're inherently unchallenging. It's just that most of the roles that I've come across don't necessarily explore that depth, and I'm looking for something that does.

summary:
just joined this new team about 1 year into their development. Demoed the work to the team about two weeks ago (half way in). Work is practically complete & runs well no issues. I create PR & assign the two PR reviewers (one my rank another a rank above me). one colleague (the one at my level) leaves some constructive comments no functional changes. The other colleague (one rank above me) says something equivalent to "does not meet our standards" "do not do x pattern since we have used y (which has a huge limitation)" to use Y pattern I would basically need to change most of the logic and it would be about 70% waste. I demoed my code with this pattern two weeks ago and there were no issues/comments from the team. The code is concise and easy to read. I had a call with the colleague and explained the code and why I used it, and showed him some other parts of the codebase where this pattern should be used, his only defense was that "it does not meet our standards because it uses X rather than y pattern, since we used y pattern in the past, we should only use y pattern" while x pattern is very similar only removing the limitation that was causing the code to be difficult to maintain etc. This "standard requirement" is written nowhere as a hard requirement and the codebase is barely one year old, with only one of the codebase founders still on the team.... I'm going to have a chat with the manager tomorrow morning.

title: Ask HN: Can I map all the arguments in a topic to "approach the truth"?
summary:
Hi HN, I wanted to take a stance on these topics people have been arguing all around. There should be some sort of answer, right?

I used to go to debates for that end. But I often only see the repetition of the same points, the hardest objection being dodged, etc. I tried AI as well, but it only returns surface level arguments likewise.

Is there anyway to preserve debate's purpose in trying to see the deepest case, while getting over these “sophistry”?

Could I map all the arguments in controversial topics (continuously allowing new inputs), and rephrase and put them in a clear sequence, so fallacies, detours, and claims already have well-established answers could be cleared out, leaving only the real tradeoff standing?

I tried it: creating TruthTree (Truthtree.app). Anything it has missed, you can hit "Challenge this claim”, type your counter, and if it's spot on (through the AI, with a fallback checker), it will be on the tree.

For example, for abortion, the map currently filters out this unanswered crux: "knowingly creating a life that depends on your body gives you a duty to continue the pregnancy."(https://truthtree.app/abortion/responsibility)

Is that the answer to abortion? What’s the map missing?

Please also let me know if this format works, and if there’s anything that could be changed to make things easier!

title: Thoughts on Nvidia from a Investors Perspective
summary:
Some thoughts on Nvidia -

Nvidia Investors should not have the false hope that Jensen Huang can prevent Nvidia’s commoditization in the long run.

Buffet -

“When a management with a reputation for brilliance tackles a business with a reputation for bad economics, it is the reputation of the business that remains intact.”

Nvidia will be around but with deteriorating economics. A parallel is Intel had unbelievable financial returns during the Wintel Duopoly, returns they have struggled to consistently maintain consistently ever since.

Firms that enable ecosystems, Intel (x86 architecture) and Nvidia (GPU) typically see unbelievable economics for a sustained period until the industry catches up and additional innovations are minor.

Also from a psychological perspective I think Huang stopped having fun when GPUs became crucial. He became a political and m&a guy vs. a demo and innovator.

title: Ask HN: Anyone know someone at GitHub to help expedite a support request?
summary:
Background: I've been working with a new company to help deliver a project. I got set up with a Google account for them (so I have myname@example.com), and I created a new Github account to associate with that email, and connected everything together.

For the first week everything was fine, I was fixing issues, putting up PRs, etc. One of the last PRs I was able to put up was a CI fix -- we had 10 CI checks that hadn't passed in months, and by fixing the underlying issue they started running. That ended up being an issue however -- they started running very long running tasks, and our Github Action minutes spiked up.

Soon after, my account was suspended, with no email, no warning, nothing. The CTO who had Github org admin access could see that I had been suspended, and nothing else. Both he on behalf of the Github Enterprise organization and myself personally submitted a ticket up, and got no response so far. We waited over the weekend, and still didn't get a response.

Since we had a deadline of before Thanksgiving, and we weren't hearing back anything from Github, my company spun me up a new Google account and Github account, just so I could start contributing. A few hours later, that account was banned as well.

It's very frustrating -- and even our Enterprise organization seems to get no recourse. Is there any good solution here?

title: Ask HN: Harness vs. Feature Factories
summary:
It seems to me the industry is at a divergence point, with strong forces pull in opposite directions.

In the "developers are team leads / checkpoint verifiers" corner we have:

- Microsoft, re "They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product" (Nadella) and "become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work"

-- Microsoft has always championed "AI as a team member", even as a product.

- Salesforce

- Stripe

- Uber, Shopify, Spotify, Meta

In the "developers use harnesses to improve personal velocity and quality corner we have:

- Netflix

- Amazon

- ... Google, but it's hard to find more than anecdotal references

These two approaches, in my view, are not compatible. Fully, or even just semi-automated feature factories keep the context, leaving the developer to validate artifacts and manage the flow, shifting responsibility to specs and building automated verifiers. It lets less technical people into the product development loop but keeps the code an AI-only territory.

On the other hand, a harness keeps the developer in control, but sacrifices velocity and requires higher technical prowess, or at least understanding, of what's being generated.

Which way is the industry going to go? Are AI-only maintained code bases going to collapse under their own weight? Are "technical" developers going to be sidelined for higher delivery velocity? Will we see two types of businesses - features and infra, each taking a polar position in this? Or even within the same business, different teams?

title: Vibe-Hackers: Script kiddies, stronger?
summary:
Hello, i am sharing a concern/opinion that i’ve been contemplating for the past couple of years. Today, we see how vibe coders with plain-english are building basic websites/webapps/mobile apps etc… you name it. Most of it is being used for good. Setting aside the quality, slop and everything else, this is not our concern. For me, the AI/agentic systems surge, directly empowered another group of people: Hackers, regardless of their nature (black hat, white hat etc…). Similar to software engineers, hackers required an immensive amount of theoretical knowledge, practical expertise and years of experience in order to be market ready (whether for an actual job or not). Script-kiddies as we know them, weren’t that meticulous in their craft , they understood some basics and executed pre-defined scripts. They didnt know how to change them, alter them or even create some their own. But today, in our new agentic-era, I believe English is the only requirement alongside a target. Considering the LLM being used is jailbroken/not safeguarded and restricted, they can literally break into systems, easily. So I was thinking to myself, a lot of people wanted to be hackers but they couldn’t (it required effort in studying, practicing etc…), today it doesnt need the same amount of effort anymore. So in the future, we are definitely going to see a surge in the number of hackers. The question comes here: How are we going to defend against malicious activities? Do we have AI-Powered systems that could act like a security analyst? Forensics? And how powerful are they? Are they deployed in reputable companies? How are they performing? Vibe-hackers are now stronger than ever, defense is required. Whether at org level or for individuals.
